Of course! GPS, or Global Positioning System, is a satellite-based navigation technology used to provide location information to devices such as smartphones, digital maps, and GPS-enabled devices. Here’s how it works: 

1. Initially, a GPS receiver on a device calculates its current location based on the GPS signals sent from three or more satellites in Earth’s orbit. 

2. The GPS receiver then compares these calculated positions to the positions of the satellites to determine the device’s accuracy in relation to the satellite that last communicated with the receiver. 

3. As GPS receivers continue to move, the accuracy is further reduced. Satellite movements are tracked on a daily basis so the new location estimate can be adjusted accordingly. To account for seasonal differences in satellite signal, the procedure is repeated on a monthly basis. This way, the most accurate position estimate is delivered to users at a given instant. 

4. GPS receivers also contain technology called “tri-pole computers” which provide additional GPS services to clients, which include high-resolution position, velocity, and time measurements. The device sends the information in the format of latitude longitude, speed and time, which are then combined and stored in the receiver in an organized fashion that GPS devices can read in real-time.

prompt: Human: Can you explain what TBI or traumatic brain injury is?
response:
Yes, I can explain what TBI or traumatic brain injury is.

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a type of physical injury that occurs to the brain. The brain is responsible for controlling and coordinating bodily functions, making it the organ of thought and memory in the human body. TBI can result from injuries to the head, neck, spine, and face, including accidents, falls, sports injuries, sports-related head injuries, and strokes.

The impact of a brain injury may vary widely, depending on the cause of the injury and the extent of damage to the brain. In some cases, the individual may suffer only short-term neurological symptoms. However, more severe traumatic brain injuries can result in long-term cognitive, psychological, and motor impairments. In some cases, TBI can lead to the development of post-traumatic seizures or brain fog, although this occurs in fewer cases. People affected by TBI are often referred to as persons with a traumatic brain injury.

Of course! Here is a delicious Lativian dish called Frikadeļu zupa, also known as Frikadels or Frikadellis. It is traditionally made with potatoes, but you can use any root vegetables you like, such as carrots or turnips. Some variations also include bacon or sausage, or sometimes both.

Ingredients:

* 2 kg potatoes, peeled and cut into 5cm cubes
* 1 kg root vegetables of your choice (carrots, turnips, yam, etc.), cut into 5cm cubes (see note below)
* 800g sliced bacon or sausages (I personally prefer bacon)
* Salt and pepper to taste
* 3 dl vegetable oil
* 1 medium onion, finely chopped
* 1 large carrot, finely chopped
* 2 garlic cloves, minced
* 2 dried bay leaves
* 3 dl white wine vinegar

Instructions:

1. Cover the root vegetables with cold water in a pot and boil them until they are very soft (about 15-20 minutes). Then drain off the water, and add some salt to taste. Allow the vegetables to cool down and then put them into a mixer or food processor along with the potatoes. You can use a food processor or even a Vitamix or any kind of blender, if you're going full "industrial."
2. Once everything is mixed well, start adding in sliced bacon or sausages. Again, I prefer bacon, personally, but if you used sausage instead they will cook together and the smell will be amazing! Also you can also add some green vegetables like kale, carrots, potatoes – whatever!
3. When everything is mixed, add in the bay leaves, 3 dl oil and vegetable mixture, 1 tablespoon each of salt and pepper. Keep mixing until everything is well combined. Don't forget to season with salt and pepper and adjust your taste if needed.
4. Preheat your oven to 200C/400F. Grease a baking dish with some oil.
5. Take some of your potato mixture and form it into one big pancake. When done cut the pancake in half and then divide both half again till everyone gets to 3 pancake layers.
6. Place layers of pancake in a baking dish. Pour some white vinegar over them to give a nice flavour.
7. Cover pancake pancake with bacon or sausage filling, then layer the pancake filling as well as some bacon or sausage filling on top and repeat pancake pancake – bacon or sausage filling, pancake pancake layer – filling and bacon or sausage filling layers again.
8. Bake in oven for 1 hour. Serve in bowls topped with sour cream and chopped onions. Optionally sprinkle with chopped parsley.

A UX portfolio is a great way for novice UX designers to showcase their skills to potential clients, showcase their work experience, and provide portfolio proof of concept to potential employers.
  
1.2. How to think of your portfolio
When creating a UX portfolio, designers should focus on presenting themselves as a strong candidate for various UX positions. They should showcase projects that show their capability in usability, interaction design, visual design, data visualization, and presentation design. Furthermore, designers should have relevant prior experience in fields like User Experience Strategy and UX Research. 

1.3. Tips for writing a UX portfolio

A well-written UX portfolio should include relevant keywords and phrases that attract potential employers to it. It includes an overview about your education and experience in the UX field, details about your role in your previous projects on different platforms like websites, mobile apps and desktop applications. One of the most important aspects of a strong UX portfolio is to list all user stories you have worked on in the last few years, to give employers an insight about your actual work done.

It also demonstrates how you have built up your skillset, your skillset as a UX design specialist and if you can be creative in using a user research methodology to shape projects. Lastly, a well thought out overview of what you expect out of a UX career can be a strong selling point of a UX portfolio. 

1.4. Why UX Portfolio Matters
A good UX portfolio is also a proof of concept that can show clients, for example, how they can use your skills with projects that they’re envisioning for implementation, such as designing interfaces for digital products or campaigns or user experience strategies to bring better digital products to market. 

1.5. Conclusion
When it comes to a UX portfolio, having a strong resume, coupled with writing a succinct description of your work experience, can go a long way in grabbing attention, showcasing your range, and demonstrating your capabilities as a UX designer. 


2. Tips for UX Portfolio Writing

2.1. Know your audience
It is important to tailor the design strategy to your intended audience, and remember that each person will have different expectations and understandings, in terms of UX design, from a portfolio.
 
2.2. Be consistent
Designers should follow a consistent format throughout each section, so that it’s easy for one to scan and review. For example the introduction should contain key information from the opening paragraph of the main sections etc. Designers should ensure the portfolio’s structure is logical and easy to scan, as well as provide an outline for further reading about UX.

2.3. Be descriptive and narrative-driven
Portfolio descriptions should use descriptive language and should demonstrate user-centered design principles, like empathy or deep understanding of users’ motivations. Designers that use storytelling to describe their work will be more likely to stand out from the crowd. A portfolio also provides an opportunity to document the user journey through different design choices you made from beginning to end.

2.4. Describe technical work, but not too much
Designers should use screenshots and/or images within a portfolio to show off functional elements but avoid too much detail. Use short paragraphs about usability features, visual style, or other elements that demonstrate the designer's creativity.

2.5. Write an outstanding description of why you should hire you
Your portfolio is your window into your UX design capabilities; by describing your motivations and qualifications in great detail with examples from previous work, you can impress employers that this is the right person for the job.

2.6. Use keywords 
Your portfolio should be easy to search for with high-quality keywords in the headline, description and tags. Examples of keywords could be “mobile app” or “web design”.

2.7. Add images and video
Using high-resolution images like images of the final design, user journey, or design mockups to engage with readers via images enhances usability. Videos and animations help bring concepts to life, showing how and why different design solutions work. It may be worth including a video describing your user stories approach as well as demonstrating some of your examples, as well as a walkthrough how your designs can impact user’s day-to-day life, demonstrating how great design can increase satisfaction and usability.   

In sum, writing a great UX portfolio is about telling stories and demonstrating your design skills. Creating an overview at the beginning can be extremely useful for you to show who you are and what you have to offer. It should be concise and use meaningful words to showcase your achievements and tell a story.  

3. Common UX Portfolio Mistakes
Some UX Designers tend to avoid writing a portfolio statement for fear of coming across too formal and academic. Rather than trying to write everything in a textbook style it’s good to focus on the most important information as it is more likely to persuade someone to hire you. 
Avoid saying nice things about people and organisations unless they can justify this approach. It may be helpful to write something about their values, motivations and what drives them and explain why clients should hire someone like them. Even if they’re very positive about you and the work you’ve done, try to leave the impression that it can’t hurt, but also be careful not to come across as self-centered and overly flattering. Also try to avoid mentioning people by name (like, ‘Chris’ or ‘Bob’ instead of by design name – it usually makes you come off as slightly fake)
Avoid making a false promise, e.g. ‘I’ve created millions of users!’ or ‘I’ll get your app ranking first.’ Instead focus on specific achievements and showcase how you can bring value to a client’s business.

As UX Designers, Sketch and Figma remain very powerful tools for creating visual designs for web and mobile apps, and make it easier to present your thinking and design vision on both ends of your workflow. 

By using Sketch as the design tool of choice you can show off the visual style, user journey, mockups, etc. but still keep the focus on the user-focused aspects of UX design. This will give potential employers and clients an idea of what you actually do and how you work, not just some pictures, screenshots etc. as with a static site. If it’s easier for you to find examples of your designs on a design tool and include links back to projects, pages etc in your portfolio this way can help make all the difference. 4. Use tools to automate the creation of visual examples of work. 
These can help speed up workflow, add automation and make your portfolio more consistent at presenting design information to an audience that doesn’t have access to visual tools like Photoshop, Sketch or Illustrator. Examples include Sketch, Figma, Canva and others.

By using tools like these you can show off your expertise in visual design. Sketch particularly, allows to create multiple layered high fidelity mockups quickly.  By including these mockups alongside your prototypes you can easily illustrate the difference between the two. Another option would be to bring screenshots onto a screen capture tool such as Camtasia, or use an online tool like Sketchbook. For teams and clients there is certainly a need for management tools to help keep a track of project progress and timelines. Tools like Trello are great project management tools that allow individuals and teams to easily organize workflows and to-do lists, track tasks, projects, deadlines, and communicate within the platform. By including a link to an overview of your own development workflow in your portfolio (as described above), you make it clear that everything you’ve done can be managed through your chosen project management tool.
  
4. Project management tools:
As an UX designer on your own, you will need to manage the UX design process yourself as well as work closely with a programmer, designer or programmer to build the features or functionalities for a UX design project. You can use Trello to help keep track of what has been completed, what needs to be finished, and next steps. Use comments and tags so that those directly responsible can easily check items off and mark deadlines they want you to complete. 

4. Use tools for testing
By using usability testing you’ll be able to demonstrate how you’ve actually tested out a design concept beforehand, how effective your approach has been and whether it has been user-friendly to navigate through all aspects of a layout or product. To save time and organize the user testing process try to use a user testing tool such as UserTesting.io.  

4. Use tools for presenting data.
When creating and sharing UX design material with stakeholders, be prepared to address statistics, analytics, or data insights to back up the evidence of a strong UX design approach and why it’s the best move. Torta de Higo Filled with Fig and Bread Pudding

What you’ll need:

For the filling:
1 lb bread, cubed

For the pudding:
1/3 cup sugar

1/3 cup honey
1 c milk
2 T water
1 egg

For the cream sauce:

2 T Water

4 T Honey

1 T Cinnamon, ground

Salt

2 T Olive oil

1 large loaf of bread, cubed

For the custard:
1/2 c egg

1/2 c milk
